questions.question: A simplified displacement-time graph for a swimmer in a 100 m race is given. Draw the corresponding velocity-time graph, showing working.
questions.answer: Velocity-time graph: a horizontal line at +1.1 m s^-1 from 0 to 45 s, a rapid change through zero at about 45 s, then a horizontal line at -1.1 m s^-1 from 45 s to 90 s.
steps: Velocity is the gradient of the displacement-time graph, so each straight section gives a constant velocity.
0 to 45 s: displacement rises from 0 to 50 m, so v = 50 / 45 = 1.1 m s^-1 (positive).
45 s to 90 s: displacement falls from 50 m back to 0, so v = -50 / 45 = -1.1 m s^-1 (she swims back).
At the turn (about 45 s) the velocity changes from +1.1 to -1.1 m s^-1 in a very short time: draw a near-vertical line through zero.
Axes: velocity in m s^-1 with values marked at +1.1 and -1.1, time to 90 s; two horizontal lines of equal length, one above and one below the time axis.

questions.question: The swimmer glides underwater for the first 15 m before using her arms and legs. Sketch the actual variation of displacement with time for the first 15 m.
questions.answer: A curve from the origin with its steepest gradient at t = 0 and a gradient that decreases as she glides; it reaches 15 m before 14 s (above the straight line from the origin to 15 m at 14 s).
steps: The simplified graph assumes constant velocity (about 1.1 m s^-1), which would take about 14 s to cover 15 m: that is the straight reference line.
The dive gives a high initial speed, so the actual graph starts with a gradient greater than 1.1 m s^-1 (steeper than the straight line).
While gliding there is no propulsion and water resistance acts, so she decelerates: the gradient decreases steadily, so the line curves over (concave down).
Because she is faster than the average at the start, she reaches 15 m in less than 14 s, so the curve ends at 15 m to the left of the 14 s mark.

questions.question: Explain one other way in which the motion of the swimmer has been simplified when drawing the displacement-time graph.
questions.answer: The graph shows constant velocity along each straight section, ignoring the changes in speed at the start, at turns and as the swimmer tires.
steps: A straight line on a displacement-time graph means constant velocity.
A real swimmer's speed changes at the start, at the turns and as she gets tired.
Drawing straight sections ignores these changes, so the graph is a simplification.

questions.question: A velocity-time graph for an object is shown. Describe how the acceleration varies with time, including calculations.
questions.answer: Acceleration is constant at about +1.6 m s^-2 from 0 to 9 s, then changes abruptly to a constant -5.1 m s^-2 after 9 s.
steps: Acceleration is the gradient of the velocity-time graph.
0 to 9 s: the line is straight from (0, 0) to (9 s, 14 m s^-1), so a = 14 / 9 = 1.6 m s^-2 (constant, positive).
After 9 s: the line is straight from (9 s, 14 m s^-1) to (17.6 s, -30 m s^-1), so a = (-30 - 14) / (17.6 - 9) = -5.1 m s^-2 (constant, negative).
So the acceleration is constant, then at 9 s it changes suddenly to a negative value with a larger magnitude (the object slows, stops at 12 s and moves backwards).

questions.question: A skydiver accelerates to terminal velocity, opens a parachute at time t1, and reaches a lower terminal velocity before landing at t2. Explain the shape of the acceleration-time graph in terms of the forces acting.
questions.answer: Acceleration falls from about g to zero at the first terminal velocity (weight = drag), becomes sharply negative when the parachute opens at t1, then returns to zero at the second, lower terminal velocity.
steps: At the start, drag is small, so the resultant force is almost the weight and the acceleration is about g (the graph starts at its maximum positive value).
As speed increases, drag increases, so the resultant (weight - drag) decreases and the acceleration falls, with a decreasing gradient, until drag = weight, resultant = 0, a = 0 at terminal velocity.
At t1 the parachute opens: the area increases suddenly, so drag becomes much greater than the weight and the resultant force is upwards, giving a large negative acceleration (a sharp negative peak).
The skydiver slows down, so drag decreases, the upward resultant reduces and the deceleration returns towards zero.

When drag again equals weight (at a smaller speed, because the drag at a given speed is now larger), the acceleration is zero at the second, lower terminal velocity, and stays at zero until landing at t2.

questions.question: The graph shows the vertical displacement of a man diving from a 12 m platform. State how the graph shows that his initial vertical velocity is zero.
questions.answer: The graph is horizontal (gradient zero) at t = 0, and the gradient of a displacement-time graph is velocity, so the initial velocity is zero.
steps: Velocity = gradient of the displacement-time graph.
At t = 0 the curve starts at 12 m with a horizontal tangent (zero gradient), so v = 0.

questions.question: A man dives from a platform 12 m above the water surface, starting from rest. Determine his vertical velocity as he enters the water.
questions.answer: v = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 12) = 15.3 m s-1 downwards.
steps: He starts with zero vertical velocity and falls 12 m with acceleration g.
Use v^2 = u^2 + 2as with u = 0, a = 9.81 m s-2 and s = 12 m.
v = sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 12) = sqrt(235.4) = 15.3 m s-1 downwards.

questions.question: Before entering the water the man has a constant vertical acceleration; after entering he has a constant vertical deceleration. Draw the velocity-time graph for his motion.
questions.answer: Straight line from (0, 0) down to about (1.5 s, -15 m s^-1) at water entry (taking up as positive), then a steeper straight line back up to zero at about 2.1 s.
steps: Before entering the water the acceleration is constant at g, so the line is straight with gradient -9.81 m s^-2 (downwards negative, as on the displacement graph), reaching about -15.3 m s^-1 after about 1.5 s.
After entering the water there is a constant deceleration, so the line is straight back up towards zero velocity.
The man stops about 4 m below the surface at about 2.1 s, so the stopping takes only about 0.6 s: the gradient is about +25 to +28 m s^-2, steeper than the first line.
Axes: the line starts at the origin and the kink is at the entry time; the final point is on the time axis at about 2.1 s.

questions.question: A constant forward force acts on a car on a straight road. After a while the speed becomes constant. Which graph shows the variation of acceleration with time? Options are graphs A to D, not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: C
steps: The driving force is constant, but resistive forces (drag) increase with speed.
The resultant force = driving force - resistive force, so it decreases as the car speeds up, and the acceleration falls.
The speed becomes constant when the resistive force equals the driving force, so the resultant is zero and the acceleration falls to zero (graph C).
A starts with zero acceleration, B ends at a non-zero acceleration (speed still increasing) and D is a constant acceleration throughout.

questions.question: A model rocket is launched with a constant upward thrust while burning fuel, then the fuel runs out and it reaches maximum height at time T. Which graph could show its acceleration against time, ignoring the mass decrease? Options are not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: C
steps: While the fuel burns, the thrust is constant (mass change neglected), so the acceleration is constant and positive.
After burnout (before time T) only gravity acts, so a = -g, constant and negative; the rocket keeps rising but slows down until it stops at the maximum height at time T.
So the graph is a constant positive value, then a sudden step down to a constant negative value before T (graph C).

A and B show a changing acceleration while the thrust acts, and in D the step is at T, which would mean the rocket is still accelerating upwards at its maximum height (where the velocity is zero), which is impossible.

questions.question: The velocity-time graph for a ball is shown. Which graph of displacement against time could represent its motion? Options A to D are not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: C
steps: Velocity increases uniformly from zero (constant acceleration), so displacement increases with an increasing gradient (a curve, starting with zero gradient).
At the dashed line the velocity changes sign (jumps), so the displacement reaches a maximum there but is continuous: no sudden jump in displacement is possible (this rules out A and B).
After the dashed line the velocity is negative and decreasing in magnitude, so displacement falls with a gradient that starts steep and flattens towards zero (curve).
D has straight lines (constant velocity) and does not show the increasing gradient, so C is the only match.

questions.question: A ball falls through air from rest. Which graph shows its displacement against time? Options A to D are graphs not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: C
steps: Falling from rest, the velocity is zero at the start and increases, so the gradient of the displacement-time graph starts at zero and gets steeper (displacement taken as negative downwards).
C starts with zero gradient and curves downwards with an increasing slope; B is a straight line (constant velocity from t = 0), D shows a decreasing gradient, and A shows no motion.

questions.question: Which row of the table gives a quantity plotted on the y-axis and the quantity represented by the gradient of the graph? The table is not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: B: y-axis velocity, gradient acceleration
steps: Gradient = change in y / change in x, so the gradient of a velocity-time graph is the change in velocity per unit time = acceleration.
The gradient of a displacement-time graph is velocity (not acceleration, so A is wrong), and the gradient of an acceleration-time graph is neither velocity nor displacement (C and D wrong).

questions.question: A car accelerates along a straight road, and the acceleration-time graph is shown. Which graph shows its velocity against time over the same interval? Graphs and options are not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: A
steps: Acceleration is positive at first, so the velocity increases; the acceleration decreases steadily, so the gradient of the velocity graph decreases.
The acceleration becomes zero at the point where the line crosses the axis, so the velocity graph has zero gradient (a maximum) at that time.
The acceleration then becomes negative, so the velocity decreases with an increasing negative gradient: a smooth concave-down curve (graph A).

questions.question: The velocity-time graph for a particle is shown. Which of A to D is the displacement-time graph for this particle? Graphs are not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: A
steps: The velocity starts positive and decreases at a constant rate, crossing zero and becoming negative: the acceleration is constant and negative.
The gradient of the displacement-time graph is the velocity, so the displacement rises with a decreasing gradient to a maximum (where v = 0), then falls with an increasing negative gradient.
This is an inverted parabola starting at the origin with a positive gradient, which is graph A.

questions.question: A velocity-time graph shows a particle with constant acceleration. P, Q and R are the magnitudes of the areas shown. Which expression gives the total displacement? A P+Q; B P+Q-R; C R+Q; D R-Q. The graph is not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: D: R - Q
steps: Displacement = area under a velocity-time graph, with areas above the time axis counted positive and areas below it negative.
P is the area above the line (not under it), so it is not part of the displacement.
R is the area under the line above the axis (positive) and Q is the area below the axis (negative), so total displacement = R - Q.

questions.question: A student walks for 6 seconds, shown on a displacement-time graph. Which row of the table gives the final displacement and velocity? The graph and table are not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: A: displacement 2.0 m, velocity 0.5 m s^-1
steps: The final displacement is read from the graph at t = 6 s: 2.0 m (the line starts at -1 m at t = 0 and crosses zero at 2 s).
Velocity = gradient = (2.0 - 0) / (6 - 2) = 0.5 m s^-1, a constant.
B's 3.0 m is the change in displacement, not the final displacement; C and D have a velocity of 2.0 m s^-1, which is not the gradient.

questions.question: A rocket accelerates horizontally due to a constant resultant force while its mass decreases as fuel is used. Which graph shows how its acceleration could change? Options A to D are graphs not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: B
steps: Constant resultant force F and decreasing mass m: a = F / m, so the acceleration must increase.
Because the mass falls steadily, 1/m increases at an increasing rate, so the graph of a against t rises (graph B), not constant (A) or decreasing (C, D).

questions.question: A ball is thrown vertically up and caught a few seconds later. Given its displacement-time graph, which graph shows its acceleration against time? Options A to D are not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: B
steps: After release the ball is in free fall: ignoring air resistance, the only force is its weight, so the acceleration is constant at g downwards for the whole flight.
Taking up as positive (as the displacement graph does), the acceleration is a negative constant: a horizontal line below the time axis (graph B).
The acceleration does not change at the top of the flight, so A (positive constant) and the sloping lines C and D are wrong.

questions.question: The graph shows how the acceleration of an object varies with time. Which graph shows how its velocity varies with time? Graphs are not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: D
steps: Velocity changes by the area under the acceleration-time graph, and the gradient of the velocity graph is the acceleration.
At t = 0 the acceleration is zero, so the velocity graph starts with zero gradient; then the acceleration increases, so the velocity graph gets steeper.
The acceleration increases at a decreasing rate to a near-constant value, so the velocity graph curves upwards with an increasing gradient (graph D).

questions.question: Students are shown a velocity-time graph for an object falling through a liquid, in which the gradient decreases. Which explanation could be a reason? A The drag force increases; B The gravitational force increases; C The temperature of the liquid increases; D The upthrust decreases.
questions.answer: A - the drag force increases.
steps: The gradient of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration.
Acceleration = (weight - upthrust - drag) / m, so the acceleration falls when the drag increases.
B would increase the acceleration, and D would increase the acceleration too.
C is not a direct cause of a smaller gradient at a given moment, so A is the reason.

questions.question: The velocity-time graph for the motion of a ball is shown. Which statement correctly describes it? A dropped and rebounds to original position; B dropped and rebounds to a lower position; C thrown upwards and caught at original position; D thrown upwards and caught at a higher position. The graph is not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: B: the ball is dropped and rebounds to a lower position
steps: The velocity starts at zero and increases uniformly in one direction, so the ball is dropped from rest and falls with constant acceleration g.
At the dashed line the velocity changes sign, so the ball hits the ground and rebounds with a smaller speed than the impact speed.
The area under the graph gives the height: the area above the axis (the fall) is bigger than the area below the axis (the rebound).
The rebound speed is less, so the ball rises to a height lower than the original height.

questions.question: Objects P and Q start at the same position at t = 0. Their velocity-time graphs are shown. Which statement describes their positions at t = 4 s? The graphs are not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: D: Q is further from the initial position than P
steps: Displacement = area under the velocity-time graph.
For P: 0 to 2 s gives +1 x 2 = +2 m, and 2 to 4 s gives -1 x 2 = -2 m, so the displacement at 4 s is 0 and P is back at the start.
For Q: the velocity is positive throughout (rising from 0 to 1 m s^-1), so the area is positive (about 3 m) and Q is away from the start.
So Q is further from the initial position than P.

questions.question: Which quantity is given by the area under a velocity-time graph? A acceleration; B displacement; C speed; D time taken.
questions.answer: B - displacement.
steps: Area under a velocity-time graph = velocity x time, which is a displacement.
The gradient of this graph gives acceleration, not the area.
Speed and time taken are not represented by the area.

questions.question: An object moves from rest with uniform acceleration for time t. X is the area under its acceleration-time graph from 0 to t. Which expression gives the distance moved? The options are not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: D: Xt/2
steps: The area under an acceleration-time graph is the change in velocity: X = at, so the final velocity v = X (starting from rest).
Distance = average velocity x time = (0 + X)/2 x t = Xt/2.

questions.question: The graph shows how the velocity of an object varies with time. Which option describes its motion? A constant acceleration; B constant displacement; C decreasing acceleration; D decreasing displacement. The graph is not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: C: decreasing acceleration
steps: The gradient of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration.
The graph is steep at the start and becomes less steep, so the gradient is decreasing: the acceleration decreases (the velocity keeps increasing, so it is not constant acceleration).
The graph does not show displacement, so B and D are not relevant.

questions.question: The displacement-time graph for a person running a race is shown. Which gives the average velocity over the race? A area between curve and x-axis from 0 to 4 h; B tangent gradient at 4 h; C tangent gradient at 2 h; D displacement at 4 h divided by 4 h.
questions.answer: D - displacement at 4 hours divided by a time of 4 hours.
steps: Average velocity = total displacement / total time.
Displacement at 4 h divided by 4 h gives this directly.
A (area) does not give velocity on a displacement-time graph.
B and C are instantaneous velocities from tangents, not averages.

questions.question: An aeroplane lands and decelerates. Its deceleration against time graph has a shaded area. What does the shaded area represent? A displacement at time t; B change in displacement during t; C velocity at time t; D change in velocity during t.
questions.answer: D - the change in velocity of the aeroplane during time t.
steps: Area under an acceleration-time graph = change in velocity.
Deceleration is the magnitude of negative acceleration, so the area is the drop in speed.
Velocity at time t and displacement are not given by this area.

questions.question: The velocity-time graph for a train journey is shown. Which expression gives the distance travelled in time 2t? The options and graph are not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: D: 5vt/2
steps: Distance = area under the velocity-time graph from 0 to 2t.
0 to t: a trapezium with parallel sides 2v and v and width t, so area = (2v + v)/2 x t = 3vt/2.
t to 2t: a rectangle of height v and width t, so area = vt.
Total distance = 3vt/2 + vt = 5vt/2.

questions.question: A person rides a bicycle along a path. At the end, the magnitude of the displacement from the start is less than the distance travelled. Describe why.
questions.answer: Displacement is the straight-line distance from start to finish, while distance is the total length of the path, which is longer because the path is not straight.
steps: Displacement is a vector: the straight-line distance and direction from the start to the end.
Distance is the total length of the route travelled.
The path changes direction, so the route length is greater than the straight-line displacement.

questions.question: The velocity-time graph for part of the bicycle ride is shown. Determine the maximum acceleration of the person.
questions.answer: About 0.27 m s^-2 (accept 0.25 to 0.30 m s^-2)
steps: Acceleration = gradient of the velocity-time graph, so the maximum acceleration is the gradient of the steepest part, from about 4 s to 16 s.
At t = 4 s the velocity is 1.8 m s^-1 and at t = 16 s it is 5.0 m s^-1 (use a large triangle on this straight section).

questions.question: An object has a constant non-zero acceleration. Which displacement-time graph could represent its motion? Options A to D are graphs not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: B
steps: A constant non-zero acceleration means the velocity changes uniformly, so the displacement-time graph has a gradient that changes uniformly: a parabola.
A and C are straight lines (constant velocity, a = 0) and D is a straight line then flat (zero acceleration apart from a sudden stop).
B is a parabola (the gradient decreases steadily from positive through zero to negative: constant negative acceleration).

questions.question: A skydiver starts from rest and moves 11 m vertically in the first 1.5 s. Air resistance is negligible if the mean acceleration is greater than 0.95 g. Deduce whether air resistance was negligible during the first 1.5 s.
questions.answer: Yes. Mean acceleration = 9.78 m s-2, which is greater than 0.95g = 9.32 m s-2, so air resistance was negligible.
steps: Starting from rest, s = 0.5at^2 gives a = 2s / t^2.
9.78 is greater than 9.32, so the air resistance was negligible during the first 1.5 s.

questions.question: The displacement-time graph for the skydiver before the parachute opens is shown. Sketch the velocity-time graph for the same period.
questions.answer: Velocity (down negative): a curve from the origin starting with gradient about -9.8 m s^-2, flattening off to a constant terminal velocity of about -45 m s^-1 (about 10 s), then horizontal until 21 s.
steps: Velocity is the gradient of the displacement-time graph: at t = 0 the gradient is zero, so the velocity graph starts at the origin.

The displacement curve gets steeper, so the speed increases, and the gradient of the velocity graph is largest at the beginning (about g), but the rate of increase falls as drag grows: the velocity curve flattens.
From about 10 s the displacement graph is a straight line, so the velocity is constant: gradient = (-800 - (-310)) / (21 - 10) = -45 m s^-1 (terminal velocity).
Sketch: start at (0, 0), curve down (negative) with decreasing steepness to a horizontal line at about -45 m s^-1 from about 10 s to 21 s.

questions.question: After jumping, the skydiver accelerates and reaches terminal velocity before opening his parachute. Explain how energy conservation applies before the parachute opens.
questions.answer: Gravitational potential energy lost equals kinetic energy gained plus energy dissipated by air resistance (thermal energy); at terminal velocity the kinetic energy is constant, so all lost potential energy becomes thermal energy.
steps: Total energy is conserved: the skydiver's loss of gravitational potential energy is the source of all other energy.
While accelerating, part of the lost potential energy becomes kinetic energy, increasing his speed.
The rest is transferred by work done against air resistance into thermal energy of the air.
At terminal velocity the kinetic energy is constant, so all the lost potential energy becomes thermal energy in the surroundings.

questions.question: After the parachute opens, the skydiver's speed changes and he reaches a new terminal velocity. Explain how the forces cause his acceleration to vary.
questions.answer: Opening the parachute increases drag above weight, giving a large upward resultant and deceleration; as speed falls, drag falls and the deceleration reduces to zero when drag equals weight at the new terminal velocity.
steps: When the parachute opens, the drag suddenly increases, so drag becomes greater than weight.
The resultant force is now upwards, so the skydiver decelerates strongly.
As his speed falls, the drag decreases, so the resultant force and deceleration get smaller.
The acceleration tends to zero as drag becomes equal to weight.
At the new terminal velocity the forces balance and the acceleration is zero.
